a2bbe9fb682a.title: Adapting Guidelines for Country use
a2bbe9fb682a.content: . The following page provides a reference to resources that can guide countries in adapting the guidelines for country use. To implement WHO recommendations in country settings, governments must interpret and then adapt the content in line with local policies, procedures, and digital tools. This implementation guide provides the generic content required in digital systems, independently of a specific software application and with the intention that countries can adapt it to meet local needs. WHO guidelines articulate and endorse rigorously tested recommendations for health interventions to be adopted within country programs. When applied correctly and consistently, guideline recommendations save lives. To ensure that countries can effectively benefit from digital health investments, the SMART Guidelines approach is intended to facilitate the accurate reflection of WHO’s clinical, public health and data use guidelines in the digital systems that countries are adopting. For more on layers of knowledge representation and how they are used in WHO’s SMART Guidelines approach, see WHO’s SMART Guidelines and this Lancet article. The standards-based technical artifacts in this implementation guide are at the third layer of knowledge representation (L3: Machine-readable recommendations). It provides code necessary for software developers to incorporate standardised logic from WHO guidelines into digital systems, testable for conformance to standards including fidelity to recommendations. A standards-based technical implementation guide builds on operational (L2) by mapping L2 content to value sets and Health Level Seven International Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards. Alongside data standards from L2, this allows for semantic and syntactic interoperability at scale. The logic derived from guidelines, which might include clinical decision support and calculations for performance indicators, which may be encoded into Clinical Quality Language (CQL). This ensures that key indicators can be consistently extracted to support patient care, as well as case surveillance and programme monitoring. The machine-readable representations in this implementation guide are intended for adaptation into countries’ digital health service delivery and reporting systems. Digital solutions comprising L3 machine-readable recommendations may then be testable for conformance to interoperability standards. The fourth layer (L4: Executable—reference applications and services) focuses on software applications and services within a digital ecosystem. It is intended to include executable reference software that accurately represents the intentions, operational, and functional requirements of the WHO recommendations; addresses user and health system needs; and comprises machine-readable data and calculations within interoperability standards, as documented in the L1–L3 layers. As a fully functional application, it is intended to serve as a generic starting point, ready to be localised to the specific operational context of the users, population, and health system within which it is deployed. Additional products at this layer include terminology services to support consistent data representation for interoperability; reusable software libraries including software development kits; application programming interfaces; and function as a service to support updates to FHIR content and capabilities across subscribed digital systems. 5273b21059d4.title: Business Processes
5273b21059d4.content: . This page describes the core business processes and workflows for the Personal Health Wallet (PHW) Implementation Guide, integrating IHE IT Infrastructure Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) v1.1.0 (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/1.1.0/) and IHE IT Infrastructure Verifiable Health Links (VHL) v1.0.0-comment (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/1.0.0-comment/). A business process is a set of related activities or tasks performed together by system actors and human personas to achieve a health information exchange objective. Each workflow below is authored in BPMN 2.0 (input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn, input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn, input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn) with full BPMN Diagram Interchange (bpmndi:BPMNDiagram) layout and rendered to SVG (input/images/PHW.A.svg, input/images/PHW.B.svg, input/images/PHW.C.svg). The data sharing agreement processes D to H, below, take the same form. Architectural Principles . | Trust-Anchor Neutrality: Every process models PKI key publication ([ITI-YY1]) and trust list retrieval ([ITI-YY2]) against an abstract Trust Anchor actor (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ActorDefinition/TrustAnchor). The WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN) is one possible Trust Anchor implementation among others (such as national health PKI roots, regional cross-border trust networks, or bilateral federation anchors). | Explicit IHE PCF and VHL Transaction Binding: Every cross-actor task names its normative IHE transaction ([ITI-108] Access Consent, [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID, [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID, [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL, [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL, [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest). | No IHE IUA Claim: Consent management and enforcement operate over IHE PCF [ITI-108] Access Consent and VHL [ITI-YY1]–[ITI-YY5] without claiming conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA [ITI-71]). | | Three-Valued Consent Decision and PROV-O Provenance: During VHL redemption (Process C), patient privacy consent directives retrieved via [ITI-108] are translated to W3C ODRL 2.2 policies (consentToOdrl()) and evaluated via three-valued decide() (permit | deny | unknown), recording a W3C PROV-O prov:Activity citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . | . Overview of Key Business Processes . The following table summarizes the three BPMN 2.0 consent and Verifiable Health Link business processes defined in this Implementation Guide. The data sharing agreement processes are summarized in their own section below. | # | Process Name | Process ID | Personas | Objectives | . | A | Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent | PHW.A | Holder, Consent Recorder, Consent Registry | Capture, update, or revoke a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry via [ITI-108] Access Consent (Post, Put, Delete). | . | B | Issue Consent-Backed Verifiable Health Link | PHW.B | Holder, VHL Sharer, Consent Registry, Trust Anchor | Register VHL Sharer signing keys with a Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY1]), verify or record active patient consent ([ITI-108]), and generate a signed Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY3]) stored in the Holder’s Personal Health Wallet. | . | C | Present and Redeem Verifiable Health Link with PCF Consent Enforcement | PHW.C | Holder, VHL Receiver, Trust Anchor, VHL Sharer, Consent Registry | Present a VHL ([ITI-YY4]), verify cryptographic trust via a Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY2]), request the manifest ([ITI-YY5]), query active PCF Consent ([ITI-108]), and enforce three-valued (permit / deny / unknown) ODRL consent evaluation with PROV-O provenance. | . Workflows . A. Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent . | Process ID: PHW.A | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn | Objective: Capture, update, or revoke a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry using the IHE PCF Access Consent [ITI-108] transaction (Post, Put, Delete), trust-anchor neutral and with no IUA claim. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.A.1 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Select base policy & disclosure scope (PCF Basic / Intermediate Consent) | Selection of base policy (Consent.policy.uri), PCFPurposeOfUseVS purpose of use, authorized actors, validity period, and clinical data scope | . | PHW.A.2 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Construct FHIR Consent & Provenance (IHE.PCF.consentBasic / Intermediate) | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, IHE.PCF.provenance | . | PHW.A.3 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Create consent directive [ITI-108] Access Consent: Post | [ITI-108] Access Consent (POST [base]/Consent or transaction Bundle with Provenance) | . | PHW.A.4 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Update or revoke directive [ITI-108] Access Consent: Put / Delete | [ITI-108] Access Consent (PUT [base]/Consent/[id] or DELETE [base]/Consent/[id]) | . | PHW.A.5 | PCF Consent Registry | Validate, version & persist Consent + Provenance [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry), assigning Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.A.6 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Confirm recorded Consent.id & versionId [ITI-108] Access Consent response | [ITI-108] Access Consent response (201 Created / 200 OK) | . Consent rules, from the person’s side . Process A is the person-side view of the data sharing agreement’s consent process (P9). The owner set four rules on 2026-10-30: . | Legal basis. Only an agreement whose legal basis is consent asks for consent. Treatment, public-health law and research waivers do not rest on consent. | Version pinning. The person consents to one fixed version of the agreement: Consent.policy.uri is that version’s URL. If the agreement is amended to widen use, the new version needs new consent. An amendment that narrows use does not. | Plain language. The person is shown the agreement’s plain-language summary, published and hashed with the agreement. That summary is what they consent to (task PHW.A.1). | Scale. Where the person has recorded nothing, the jurisdiction’s chosen PCF implicit default policy applies: opt-in (for example Policy-deny) or opt-out (for example Policy-basic-normal or Policy-all-normal). Registry lookups may be cached (task PHW.C.5), but withdrawing a Consent (status becomes inactive, task PHW.A.4) ends every cached result that holds it at once. | . B. Issue Consent-Backed Verifiable Health Link . | Process ID: PHW.B | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn | Objective: Publish VHL Sharer PKI signing keys to an abstract Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY1]), verify or record an active patient privacy consent directive ([ITI-108]), and generate a signed Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY3]) for storage in the Holder’s Personal Health Wallet. Trust-anchor neutral (WHO GDHCN is one possible Trust Anchor among others). | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.B.1 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Submit Sharer PKI signing key [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID | [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/PublishPKIMaterial) | . | PHW.B.2 | Trust Anchor (e.g. GDHCN, national, or regional anchor) | Publish key in Trust Anchor trust list [ITI-YY1] (GDHCN or other anchor) | [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/CapabilityStatement/IHE.VHL.TrustAnchor) | . | PHW.B.3 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Request VHL generation [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL ($generate-vhl) | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/OperationDefinition/GenerateVHL) | . | PHW.B.4 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Query or record active Consent [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search / Post | [ITI-108] Access Consent (GET [base]/Consent?patient=...&status=active or POST [base]/Consent) | . | PHW.B.5 | PCF Consent Registry | Return active PCF Consent (Consent.id + versionId) [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry) | . | PHW.B.6 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Assemble & sign VHL payload bound to Consent [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL (IHE.VHL.VHLSharer), signing with [ITI-YY1] key material | . | PHW.B.7 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Store signed VHL in Personal Health Wallet [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL response received by VHLHolder | . C. Present and Redeem Verifiable Health Link with PCF Consent Enforcement . | Process ID: PHW.C | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn | | Objective: Present a Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY4]), verify cryptographic signatures against a Trust Anchor’s trust list ([ITI-YY2]), request the health document manifest ([ITI-YY5]), query active PCF Consent ([ITI-108]), and enforce three-valued (permit | deny | unknown) ODRL consent evaluation with W3C PROV-O decision provenance. Trust-anchor neutral (WHO GDHCN is one possible Trust Anchor among others) and makes no IUA claim. | . | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.C.1 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Present VHL payload to Receiver [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL | [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/UtilizeVHL) | . | PHW.C.2 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Request Trust Anchor key list [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID | [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/RetrievePKIMaterial) | . | PHW.C.3 | Trust Anchor (e.g. GDHCN, national, or regional anchor) | Return signed trust list [ITI-YY2] (GDHCN or other Trust Anchor) | [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID (IHE.VHL.TrustAnchor) | . | PHW.C.4 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Verify VHL signature & request manifest [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/RequestVHLDocuments) | . | PHW.C.5 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Query active patient Consent [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search | [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search (GET [base]/Consent?patient=...&status=active) | . | PHW.C.6 | PCF Consent Registry | Return active PCF Consent Bundle [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry), returning Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.C.7 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Evaluate PCF Consent (ODRL decide: permit / deny / unknown) & PROV-O log | consentToOdrl() + three-valued decide() (permit | deny | unknown) + W3C PROV-O prov:Activity citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.C.8 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Return authorized manifest & documents [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (permit) | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (200 OK Bundle of DocumentReference / clinical resources when decision is permit) | . | PHW.C.9 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Refuse disclosure with OperationOutcome [ITI-YY5] (deny or unknown) | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (403 Forbidden OperationOutcome when decision is deny or unknown) | . | PHW.C.10 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Process clinical documents or refusal notice [ITI-YY5] response | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest consumer (IHE.VHL.VHLReceiver) | . Data Sharing Agreement Processes (Server to Server) . Processes D to H implement a data sharing agreement (DSA) between a data provider and a data recipient. Each one is a technical process from the DSA process analysis for folio-assistant#2702 (P4, P5, P11, P12 and P13). The owner chose this IG as their home on 2026-10-30 (19:59Z). They apply to every agreement, whether it is computable (a W3C ODRL 2.2 Agreement derived from the legal text) or document-only (a signed PDF). The only difference is where the access rule comes from: the ODRL Agreement, or a configuration an administrator sets by hand from the PDF. What every process relies on: . | The agreement’s fixed-version URL. Each agreement version is published at an immutable URL, with its SHA-256, and catalogued as a DCAT 3 dcat:Distribution with spdx:checksum (DCAT 3 §6.8, §6.8.20). For a computable agreement this URL is also the ODRL uid. Tokens, grants, Consents and audit records cite this URL, never a “latest” URL. | Grants are W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0. A grant cites the agreement through relatedResource (VC DM 2.0 §5.3), and its status is a W3C Bitstring Status List entry. litlfred/smart-trust-tools verifies it. | Pluggable trust anchors. WHO GDHCN is one option. The others are a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list. UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA, is approved (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z) for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication, which fits a national X.509 PKI as the anchor. OpenID Federation is out of scope. | No invented fields. Where no standard has a slot, the text says so as a gap or open point. | . | # | Process Name | Process ID | DSA process | Objectives | . | D | Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.D | P4 | Register the recipient’s server as an OAuth client (RFC 7591, UDAP via HL7 SSRAA, or by an administrator), authenticated by mTLS (RFC 8705) or a JWT assertion (RFC 7523; with UDAP, private_key_jwt with an x5c chain), and record which agreement versions it may act under. | . | E | Server-to-Server Access under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.E | P5 | Issue a short-lived, key-bound token (DPoP, RFC 9449) for an RFC 9396 authorization_details request whose identifier (§2.2) is the agreement’s fixed-version URL, after the access decision. | . | F | Access Decision under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.F | P11 | Run permits() on the verified grant and the agreement. A consent-based agreement also needs an active PCF Consent. The result is permit, deny or unknown, and unknown is never permit. | . | G | Audit, Provenance and Duty Checks under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.G | P12 | Record each decision as a W3C PROV-O record that cites the agreement, and as an IHE ATNA audit event ([ITI-20]). Record duty fulfilment and review it. | . | H | Revocation and Suspension under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.H | P13 | Stop grants (Bitstring Status List), tokens and clients (RFC 7009), and keys (trust list or CRL). | . In the tables, † marks a section number cited from standing knowledge and not re-checked when this page was written. The RFC 9396, RFC 9449, RFC 8693, W3C VC 2.0, W3C Bitstring Status List and DCAT 3 sections were checked against the published specifications on 2026-10-30. D. Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement . | Process ID: PHW.D | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.D.bpmn | Objective: Register the data recipient’s server as an OAuth client of the data provider’s authorization server. It is bound to a key published under a trust anchor the agreement accepts, and to the agreement versions it may act under. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | Standard and section | . | PHW.D.1 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | Prepare client key or certificate under an accepted trust anchor | Key published under an accepted anchor (DSA P3): DID Core 1.0 + did:web, or RFC 5280 | . | PHW.D.2 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | Send dynamic client registration request (RFC 7591) | RFC 7591 §3.1†; private_key_jwt metadata RFC 7523 §2.2†; tls_client_auth RFC 8705 §2.1†. RFC 7592 is Experimental and needs owner approval | . | PHW.D.3 | Data Provider Administrator (person) | Enter client by hand, scopes from the signed agreement text | Document-only route. The change record cites the agreement URL and its SHA-256 | . | PHW.D.4 | Provider Authorization Server | Validate client key or certificate against the accepted trust anchor | DID document, RFC 5280 §6† path validation, or a local list. UDAP route: UDAP DCR §4‡ (SSRAA §3.2.3): software statement signature, x5c chain to the trust community’s anchor, requested parameters | . | PHW.D.5 | Trust Anchor (GDHCN or another accepted anchor) | Return trust list or certificate status | GDHCN did:web:tng-cdn.who.int:v2:trustlist; CRL RFC 5280 §5† | . | PHW.D.6 | Provider Authorization Server | Record which agreement versions the client may act under | Gap: neither RFC 7591 nor the SSRAA software statement has a field for this, so it is the server’s own configuration. Two more expressions, outside the table, give evaluatedPolicies (every policy) and permittingPolicies (the applicable ones that permitted) for the duties and the audit. Why PRIORITY. The owner’s order (any deny, then any unknown, then any permit, then none applicable) is a ranking of outcomes, and PRIORITY is the DMN hit policy that returns the matching rule whose output comes first in the output’s ordered outputValues. Each rule then states one condition, and the ranking resolves overlaps; for example, a request with a deny and an unknown matches rules 1 and 3, and "deny" wins. Rules with the same output never overlap (rules 1 and 2 differ in conflictStrategy), so the result does not depend on rule order. COLLECT was not used: its aggregators (SUM, MIN, MAX, COUNT) work on numbers, so the outcomes would have to be coded as numbers that no standard defines. FIRST would also work, but it hides the ranking in the rule order. Every combination of up to three policies, with every outcome and strategy, was checked against the owner’s rule, and exactly one outcome results each time. Why only one table. Each row is decided by decide() for that policy alone (PHW.F.10, with the PCF Consent path of PHW.F.8), and applicability is a check of the ODRL target, purpose and assignee. Neither is a decision table, so there is no per-row DMN table. The DMN decision combines the rows once per request. Override 1: the policies. ODRL 2.2 lets each policy declare a conflict strategy with odrl:conflict: odrl:perm (permissions override prohibitions), odrl:prohibit (prohibitions override permissions) or odrl:invalid (the policy is void if any conflict is detected). These terms were checked against the ODRL 2.2 vocabulary and the pinned JSON-LD context (folio-assistant-core scripts/test-fixtures/dsa-contexts/odrl-2.2.context.json). When every applicable policy declares the same strategy, the table uses it. A policy that declares none counts as prohibit, the owner’s default D. If the applicable policies declare different strategies, conflictStrategy is invalid. ODRL 2.2 says a policy with several conflict values (after a merge or inheritance) is void when its rules conflict (W3C ODRL Information Model 2.2, Policy Conflict Strategy). This IG treats the applicable policies of one request as merged. The only declaration that changes an outcome is perm declared by every applicable policy. ODRL’s own default when nothing is declared is invalid, but the outcome is the same: with a conflict, invalid voids the policy and prohibit denies, and both are refused. Open points (owner): . | The lookup has no standard element. No existing VHL, OAuth or VC element maps a verified receiver to an agreement. The mapping is the Sharer’s own configuration, keyed by the agreement’s fixed-version URL, the same configuration as PHW.D.6. No field is invented. | Several agreements with one receiver. Decided (owner, 2026-11-01 07:54Z, card Q-DRAIN-4, option D; 07:55Z, overridable default). Every agreement and Consent held with the receiver is evaluated, and one that does not cover the request is not applicable. The results are combined by the DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess: by default permit if at least one applicable policy permits and none prohibits (ODRL 2.2 odrl:prohibit). Policies may declare another odrl:conflict, and a deployer may replace the decision under the same contract. The duties of every permitting agreement apply, and the audit cites every agreement evaluated. | Purpose of use in the audit event. With the SSRAA option, the purpose can come from the token request: purpose_of_use, a required array of codes in the hl7-b2b extension of the receiver’s JWT client assertion (SSRAA §5.2.1.1; HL7 v3 PurposeOfUse is encouraged, §5.2.1.2). SSRAA does not constrain the access token’s format (§5.2.3), so the Sharer has the purpose directly when its own authorization server issued the token; how a separate authorization server would pass it on is not specified. Without SSRAA, [ITI-YY5] carries no purpose, and it comes from the agreement or from the PCF Consent recorded at [ITI-YY3] (Consent.provision.purpose). Which source the event records, and which one wins when they differ, is open. | Possible ballot comments. The VHL Verifiable Credential Option example uses issuanceDate and expirationDate, which are VC 1.1 terms. VC 2.0 uses validFrom and validUntil. In the OAuth with SSRAA Option example (ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.4), the decoded client assertion gives purpose_of_use as a single string, where SSRAA §5.2.1.1 requires an array, and the token request omits the udap=1 parameter that SSRAA §5.2.2.2 requires. VHL says its workflow is informative and SSRAA takes precedence. | consent_policy in hl7-b2b. Decided (owner, 2026-11-01 07:54Z, card Q-DRAIN-4, option D). SSRAA §5.2.1.1 lets a client name policy URIs in consent_policy, an optional array, and FHIR Consent URLs in consent_reference. A receiver MAY list one or more agreements’ fixed-version URLs in consent_policy. This narrows the permissions it acts under (PHW.I.4) but never escapes another applicable agreement’s prohibition. Naming is optional, so the HTTP Message Signatures and Verifiable Credential options, which have no such field, still work. Nothing is added to any standard. | . Shared Certificate Processes . These two processes are shared blocks for any certificate type (BPMN reuse proposal, Q-BPMN-1 A). A trust domain or another IG calls them instead of copying their steps. Their steps come from the smart-icvp issuing and verifying diagrams. | # | Process Name | Process ID | Objectives | . | J | Issue a Verifiable Digital Health Certificate | PHW.J | Ask the holder for consent, collect what the certificate profile (a data input) needs, issue and sign the certificate, issue its VHL (process B), and deliver it to the wallet. | . | K | Verify a Certificate and its Status | PHW.K | Receive the claim; redeem a VHL through process C, check by hand, or decode the QR code, get the issuer key from the Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY2]), verify the signature, and check the registry. | . J. Issue a Verifiable Digital Health Certificate . | Process ID: PHW.J | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.J.bpmn | Objective: Shared block B4 of the BPMN reuse proposal (Q-BPMN-1 A, 2026-11-01): one issuing process for every certificate type. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | Source | . | PHW.J.1 | Certificate Issuer (health worker or issuing system) | J1. Inform the holder and ask for consent to issue | smart-icvp: ‘Inform traveller and request consent to digitize’ and ‘Counsel patient on consent’. This is consent to issue the certificate. Consent to share it later is recorded by process A and checked by process B. | . | PHW.J.2 | Certificate Issuer (health worker or issuing system) | J2. Collect the data the certificate profile needs | smart-icvp: ‘Capture Vaccination Data’, ‘Collate ICVP data’, ‘Conduct data entry from physical card into system’. What is collected is set by the certificate profile input. | . | PHW.J.3 | Certificate Issuance Service | J3. Issue and sign the certificate | smart-icvp: ‘Issue Digital ICVP Card’. 752d4435184f.content: . Key concepts and abbreviations are described here. Additional terms are defined in the Glossary and List of Abbreviations in the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for [insert health domain here] (link forthcoming) . Concepts . | Term | Description | . | Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical code (ATC) | A unique code assigned to a medicine according to the organ or system it works on and how it works. | . | Certificate | A document attesting a fact. In the context of the vaccination certificate, it attests to the fact that a vaccine has been administered to an individual. | . | Clinical practice guidelines (CPG) | Clinical practice guidelines are statements that include recommendations intended to optimize patient care that are informed by a systematic review of evidence and an assessment of the benefits and harms of alternative care options. | . | Clinical Quality Language (CQL) | This is a HL7 specification for the expression of clinical knowledge that can be used within both the Clinical Decision Support (CDS) and Clinical Quality Measurement (CQM) domains. | . | Data dictionary | A centralized repository of information about the data elements that contains their definition, relationships, origin, usage, and type of data. For this digital adaptation kit, the data dictionary is provided as a spreadsheet. | . | Data element | A unit of data that has specific and precise meaning. | . | Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) | A standard describing data formats and elements and an application programming interface for exchanging electronic health records. | . | Functional requirement | Capabilities the system must have in order to meet the end-users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process. | . | Implementation Guide (IG) | A set of rules about how FHIR resources are used (or should be used) to solve a particular problem, with associated documentation to support and clarify the usage. This IG is based on WHO guidance, as it is represented in the Digital Adaptation Kit for [insert health domain here], to support the adoption of open standards for interoperability. | . | Indicator | Summary measures that capture relevant information on different attributes and dimensions of health status and performance of a health system. | . | International Patient Summary (IPS) | An electronic health record extract containing essential healthcare information about a client. | . | Non-functional requirement | General attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. 6531c86ae786.title: data-models-and-exchange
6531c86ae786.content: . This section contains the data models and data exchange protocols with actors and transactions defined. It is part of the L3 machine-readable knowledge representation. The pages included in this section are described below. | Actors - A list and description of software or human entities that interact with the system, derived from business requirements defined in the L2. | Sequence Diagrams - Sequence diagrams depicting the interactions between system actors, in order, derived from business processes in the L2. | Transactions - A defined list of system transactions at an atomic level for each actor along with narrative, capability statements, structure definition, questionnaires, document bundles and composition. It may also refer to transactions in other implementation guides. | Logical Models - A StructureDefinition resource that describes data element definitions and their associated rules of usage, derived from the data dictionary in the L2. | Indicators and Measures - A thematic list of indicators defined in the implementation guide that link to L1 and L2 guidance documents. | . Design Documentation -DRAFT- . The documentation below details how to use this IG to execute the decision logic and the resources required to do so including PlanDefinitions, ActivityDefinitions, ValueSets, and Libraries. PlanDefinitions . insert content here has been represented as a FHIR PlanDefinition conformant to the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Implementation guide CPG-ComputablePlanDefinition. For example, there is a PlanDefinition for Hepatitis A, Measles, etc. The intention behind this design is for each implementation to utilize only the antigens that are required for their national/local context, as many countries have national vaccine routines, which may leverage the WHO guidance. The aim of this content was to be adaptable for those contexts. These PlanDefinitions can be found in the Artifact Index . ActivityDefinitions . To represent the activities that need to be carried out, this implementation guide follows the workflow patterns established by the base FHIR specification. Each antigen represented as a PlanDefinition will be processed to produce ActivityDefnitions conform to the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Implementation guide CPG-ActivityProfiles. FHIR Library . The FHIR Library contains a base64 encoded CQL library which represents the decision logic as a series of boolean clauses. Each PlanDefinition and Measure will reference a Library from which each decision point can be made and specify which expression from the CQL is used to trigger a decision in PlanDefinition or where to retrieve data to create the MeasureReport in the Measure, repsectively. ValueSets . Many of the ValueSets used in this IG are from CPG on FHIR and the IPS. There are a number of generated ValueSets based on the user scenarios detailed in this IG. There is one exception to that format which is the vaccine libraries, which map the codes between a variety of different systems including SNOMED GPS and WHO ATC in order to allow implementers to search for any vaccine which might be applicable to their user. More details on this approach is provided below. Edit this page on GitHub . | <prev | top | next> . IG © 2023+ WHO. Package smart.who.int.trust-phw#0.1.0 based on FHIR 5.0.0. The structure of the decision-support tables is based on an adaptation of the Decision Model and Notation (DMN™), an industry standard for modelling and executing decision logic. These decision-support tables detail the business rules, data inputs and outputs to support EIR business processes. Overview of decision support tables . d6d2201ac36b.title: Worked Example: IPS Pilgrimage (Hajj)
d6d2201ac36b.content: . This page is a worked example. It applies the business processes A, B, C, F and I of this guide to one case: the IPS Pilgrimage (Hajj) implementation guide (smart-ips-pilgrimage, FHIR R4, IHE PCF 1.1.0). It follows the analysis written for folio-assistant#2702 on 2026-10-30. The case: during Hajj, the host country (KSA) is the VHL Receiver. It asks the pilgrim’s origin country (for example Malaysia) for the pilgrim’s International Patient Summary (IPS) over a Verifiable Health Link (VHL). The origin country’s health information exchange (HIE) is the VHL Sharer. The IPS carries two consent statements from the pilgrim, and those two Consents are the policy for the exchange. The page does not change the IPS Pilgrimage guide. The gaps below say what that guide, or the specifications it uses, would need. Gap G1 has since been resolved in that guide by smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. The pilgrim’s consents are the policy . For Hajj, there is no separate data sharing agreement for the Sharer to look up. The pilgrim’s two Consents are the policy, and each is coded in Consent.policyRule (owner, Q-DRAIN-5, 2026-11-01 07:44Z). That is how the IPS Pilgrimage guide models them since smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. policyRule holds a code from that guide’s IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT CodeSystem, with coding.version set to the CodeSystem version whose consent text the pilgrim was shown. Any arrangement between KSA and the origin country, such as a memorandum of understanding, stays outside the computable decision. Each Consent binds the party it names: . | Consent | What it allows | Who is bound, and where it is checked | . | Origin release (CONSENT-<origin>, for example CONSENT-MYS) | The origin HIE may release the IPS to the KSA Ministry of Health, as information recipient, for treatment, during the Hajj period. | The origin HIE. It enforces this Consent from its own Consent Registry ([ITI-108]) at step 10. The Consent’s decide() result is one row of the default DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess (PHW.F.10). | . | Host use (CONSENT-KSA) | The KSA Ministry of Health may use the IPS for care during Hajj and any follow-up. | KSA, which follows it after receipt (step 14). The origin does not enforce it. | . The receiver is identified by trust: its key or certificate is accepted in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain (PHW.I.2, PHW.I.3). There is no agreement lookup at PHW.I.4. “Patient-mediated” then means three things, each an existing mechanism: . | The pilgrim records the consents (PCF [ITI-108], process A). | The pilgrim carries the link (the VHL QR code, [ITI-YY4], process C). | The pilgrim is present at the encounter. Giving the passcode (the VHL P flag; ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.5.8) is the in-person act. | . The registry copy is enforced; the IPS copy is evidence. The IPS Bundle also carries copies of both Consents. They travel with the data as evidence for KSA. The Sharer does not enforce them: it enforces the copy in its own Consent Registry. The IPS is signed once, when it is issued, so its copy cannot show a later withdrawal (consent rule 4). The flow, step by step . The Hajj encounter, mapped onto VHL and onto the activities of this guide. Steps that hit a gap name it; the gaps are listed in the next section. Before Hajj . | # | Step | Actor | PHW activities | Transaction | Gap | . | 1 | Trust. The origin HIE publishes its signing keys to the ips-pilgrimage trust domain. GDHCN is the trust anchor here, as one option among others. KSA must also publish its own keys or certificates there, so that the origin can authenticate it at step 9. | Origin HIE, Trust Anchor | PHW.B.1, PHW.B.2 | [ITI-YY1] | G3 | . | 2 | Registration. With the OAuth with SSRAA option, KSA’s EMR registers with the origin HIE by UDAP (HL7 SSRAA), using a certificate that chains to an anchor of the ips-pilgrimage trust domain. With HTTP Message Signatures, nothing is registered: the origin reads KSA’s key from the trust list. No agreement URL is involved. | Origin HIE, KSA EMR | PHW.D.9, PHW.D.10 | — | G3 | . | 3 | Counselling and consent. A counsellor explains the plain-language text of each consent (consent rule 3). The wallet records both Consents in the origin’s Consent Registry. Each Consent’s policyRule names which Hajj consent it is (CONSENT-<origin> or CONSENT-KSA), and its coding.version names the IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT version whose text the pilgrim was shown. That version pins the text, which is the role consent rule 2 gives policy.uri elsewhere. | Pilgrim, Consent Recorder, Consent Registry | PHW.A.1, PHW.A.2, PHW.A.3, PHW.A.5, PHW.A.6 | [ITI-108] |   | . | 4 | IPS. The origin HIE generates the Hajj IPS Bundle, with both Consents as entries, and signs it. | Origin HIE | — (IPS Pilgrimage guide) | — | G2 | . | 5 | VHL. The wallet asks for a VHL with a passcode and an expiry. The Sharer checks that the Consents are active, then signs the link. The link’s expiry should not run past the Consents’ provision.period. | Pilgrim, Origin HIE | PHW.B.3, PHW.B.4, PHW.B.5, PHW.B.6, PHW.B.7 | [ITI-YY3], [ITI-108] |   | . At the encounter in KSA . | # | Step | Actor | PHW activities | Transaction | Gap | . | 6 | The pilgrim shows the QR code and gives the passcode. | Pilgrim | PHW.C.1 | [ITI-YY4] |   | . | 7 | The KSA EMR verifies the HCERT/CWT signature against the trust list. | KSA EMR, Trust Anchor | PHW.C.2, PHW.C.3, PHW.C.4 | [ITI-YY2] |   | . | 8 | The KSA EMR registers the pilgrim with the pilgrimage number. | KSA EMR | — (IPS Pilgrimage guide, step 03) | — |   | . | 9 | The KSA EMR sends Retrieve Manifest with the passcode, authenticated by one VHL option. The IPS Pilgrimage guide uses mTLS node authentication ([ITI-19]) today, which is not one of VHL’s options. | KSA EMR | PHW.I.1 | [ITI-YY5] | G3, G4, G5 | . | 10 | The origin HIE decides. (a) It authenticates KSA by trust in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain. There is no agreement lookup: the Consents are the policy. (b) It searches its own registry for the pilgrim’s active origin-release Consent (policyRule = CONSENT-<origin>). (c) It evaluates that Consent with decide() (see the conditions below). The result is the Consent’s row in the default DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess, whose outcome routes the request. (d) Anything missing gives unknown, and unknown is never permit. | Origin HIE, Consent Registry | (a) PHW.I.2, PHW.I.3; (b) PHW.I.5 → PHW.F.8, PHW.F.9; (c) PHW.F.10; (d) PHW.F.11, PHW.I.6 or PHW.I.7 | [ITI-YY5], [ITI-YY2], [ITI-108] | G2 | . | 11 | Audit. The origin HIE records an audit event. It cites the governing Consents by policyRule code and CodeSystem version, the id and meta.versionId of each Consent read for the decision, which of them permitted, the DMN decision used, the receiver, the purpose, and the documents released or the refusal. | Origin HIE, writing to the Audit Record Repository | PHW.I.9 (with PHW.G.1) | [ITI-20] |   | . | 12 | The origin HIE returns the List and its DocumentReferences (_include=List:item, VHL’s Include DocumentReference Option), then the IPS. | Origin HIE | PHW.I.6 | [ITI-YY5], [ITI-68] |   | . | 13 | The KSA EMR verifies the IPS signature, stores a copy and shows it. | KSA EMR | PHW.I.11 | — |   | . | 14 | KSA follows CONSENT-KSA after receipt. Its duties (for example, keep the IPS for follow-up care only) come from that Consent’s text. Nothing machine-readable travels with the document to say so yet. | KSA Ministry of Health | process G (PHW.G.5, PHW.G.6) | — | G6 | . When does step 10 permit? Only when every one of these holds: . | the passcode is valid; | the link has not expired; | the origin-release Consent is active in the origin’s own registry; | the KSA Ministry of Health, as verified by trust in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain, is the consented actor (provision.actor); | the purpose is treatment (provision.purpose = TREAT); | today is inside the Hajj period (provision.period). | . The origin-release Consent is found by its policyRule code (CONSENT-<origin>), and its coding.version names the consent text the pilgrim was shown. The KSA-use Consent binds KSA, not the origin, so the origin does not need it to permit. With only one Consent applicable, the default DMN decision returns that Consent’s own result. Gaps . Ordered by how much each one blocks a computable decision. Each row names the existing standard that would close it. Nothing here invents a field. | Gap | What is missing | What would close it | . | G1. The Hajj consents are not computable as written. Resolved by smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. | Was: the consent type sat in provision.purpose, the examples had display names only, and policyRule.text was "some policy", so decide() would return unknown every time. Still open in that guide: the consent texts for two origin countries (CONSENT-IDN, CONSENT-OMN) are placeholders (consent rule 3). | HajjConsent now requires policyRule with an IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT code and coding.version (CodeSystem version 2.1.0). policyRule also satisfies R4 invariant ppc-1, so no policy.uri is needed. It also requires provision.actor (an Organization by identifier, role IRCP), provision.purpose from v3 PurposeOfUse (TREAT), and provision.period. See the examples below. | . | G2. Which copy of a consent counts. | The specifications do not say whether the Sharer enforces the registry copy or the copy inside the IPS, or what KSA should do with its copy. | A rule in the implementation guide, not a new field: the Sharer enforces the registry copy (PCF [ITI-108]); the IPS copy is evidence, carrying its meta.versionId so that KSA can cite it. | . | G3. mTLS is not a VHL option. | The IPS Pilgrimage guide’s sequence diagram still authenticates the KSA node with mTLS ([ITI-19]). Since smart-ips-pilgrimage#3, its transaction page says that mTLS is not one of VHL [ITI-YY5]’s three options and recommends OAuth with SSRAA. How KSA’s certificate or key is published in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain is still not specified. | Choose one VHL option: OAuth with SSRAA (UDAP), approved for process D and I, which is X.509-based like mTLS; or HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). KSA publishes the matching key in the trust domain ([ITI-YY1]). | . | G4. The facility and the clinician are invisible. | CONSENT-KSA is limited to healthcare facilities in the Hajj district, but the request comes from one national KSA EMR. With HTTP Message Signatures, the Sharer sees only KSA, so it cannot check the district limit and the audit cannot name who looked. | HL7 SSRAA: the hl7-b2b extension carries organization_id and the requesting user (SSRAA §5.2.1.1). | . | G5. The purpose of use is not carried. | [ITI-YY5] has no purpose parameter, so the decision assumes TREAT from the Consent’s provision.purpose. This is open point 3 of process I. | HL7 SSRAA purpose_of_use in hl7-b2b (SSRAA §5.2.1.1), with HL7 v3 PurposeOfUse codes. | . | G6. KSA’s duties after receipt are not machine-readable. | CONSENT-KSA allows “any follow up care” and says nothing about retention or onward sharing. Nothing in VHL, IPS or PCF carries such obligations with the document. | Either HL7 Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) obligation codes in meta.security (needs owner approval: not final), or, with approved standards only, KSA keeps following the CONSENT-KSA text it is bound by and audits against it in process G, with no labels on the document. | . | G7. What the audit event cites. Resolved by smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. | Was: the IPS Pilgrimage guide had [ITI-20] at the origin HIE but did not say what the event contains. | That guide now states it, as process I gives it (PHW.I.9): the Consents by policyRule code and CodeSystem version, each Consent’s id and meta.versionId, receiver, purpose and documents released or the refusal. KSA, as an ATNA Secure Node (VHL Vol 1 §1:XX.3), also audits what it receives. IHE BALP patterns need owner approval. | . | G8. Break the glass has no VHL. | In phase 2 of the IPS Pilgrimage guide (process 5.0) the pilgrim may be unconscious: no QR code and no passcode, so the lookup is by pilgrimage number, outside VHL entirely. | Its own search transaction (likely IHE PDQm [ITI-78] with IHE MHD [ITI-67]), a separate opt-in Consent (the wallet’s “break the glass” setting), and the emergency purpose of use ETREAT. Not specified today. | . | G9. Versions and status. | The IPS Pilgrimage guide does not depend on VHL. It describes the VHL steps in its own transaction pages, partly in older SMART Health Links wording (“modified ITI-67”). Its HajjConsent notes on FHIR R5 (verification.verifiedBy, Consent.period) are for later. | Depend on IHE VHL and cite it as what it is: 1.0.0-comment, a public-comment ballot. The guide’s _include=List:item already matches VHL’s Include DocumentReference Option. FHIR R4 with PCF 1.1.0 already matches the approved PCF version. | . Example consents . The two Consents below match the HajjConsent examples of smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. They are FHIR R4 resources on the IHE PCF 1.1.0 profile IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, which HajjConsent is built on. This guide is built on FHIR R5, where Consent has no policyRule, so they are given here as FSH and are not instances of this guide. They were compiled with SUSHI 3.21.0 against hl7.fhir.r4.core 4.0.1 and ihe.iti.pcf 1.1.0, with no errors. Every name, identifier, URL and date is a fictional example: . | The pilgrim, the Malaysian HIE and the Saudi Ministry of Health are stand-ins, as in smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. Their identifiers are example.org URLs. | 2025-05-01 to 2025-08-31 stands in for the Hajj period (Hajj 1446/2025, as the IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT 2.1.0 text says), with time for follow-up care. | . Both Consents permit the same recipient, for the same purpose and period. They differ in which Hajj consent they are (policyRule), and so in the text the pilgrim was shown (sourceAttachment) and in whom they bind: the first lets the origin release the IPS, and the second lets the host use it. Only existing elements are used: policyRule (with coding.version), provision.actor, provision.purpose and provision.period. There is no policy.uri, because there is no separate agreement. Alias: $PCFIntermediate = https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate Alias: $v3-ActReason = http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason Alias: $v3-ParticipationType = http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ParticipationType Alias: $consentscope = http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope Alias: $LOINC = http://loinc.org Alias: $IPSHajjConsent = http://smart.who.int/ips-pilgrimage/CodeSystem/IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT // FHIR R4 (4.0.1) and IHE PCF 1.1.0. All names, identifiers and URLs are fictional examples. // The Consents are the policy: policyRule names which Hajj consent each one is, with the // IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT CodeSystem version whose text the pilgrim was shown (smart-ips-pilgrimage#3). Instance: PilgrimExample InstanceOf: Patient Title: "Pilgrim (fictional)" Usage: #example * identifier.system = "https://hie.mys.example.org/fhir/sid/pilgrimage-number" * identifier.value = "PILG-0000-0001" * name.family = "Example" * name.given = "Amina" * gender = #female * birthDate = "1970-01-01" Instance: OriginHIEExample InstanceOf: Organization Title: "Origin country HIE (fictional): Sharer and Consent Registry custodian" Usage: #example * identifier.system = "urn:ietf:rfc:3986" * identifier.value = "https://hie.mys.example.org/" * name = "Ministry of Health Malaysia Health Information Exchange (example)" Instance: HostMoHExample InstanceOf: Organization Title: "Host country Ministry of Health (fictional): VHL Receiver" Usage: #example * identifier.system = "urn:ietf:rfc:3986" * identifier.value = "https://moh.ksa.example.org/" * name = "Ministry of Health Saudi Arabia (example)" Instance: PilgrimConsentOriginRelease InstanceOf: $PCFIntermediate Title: "Pilgrim consent: the origin HIE may release the IPS to the host Ministry of Health" Description: "The first of the pilgrim's two Hajj consents (CONSENT-MYS, origin release). Permit, to the host Ministry of Health as information recipient, for treatment, during the example Hajj period. The origin HIE enforces it from its own Consent Registry." Usage: #example * status = #active * scope = $consentscope#patient-privacy * category[0] = $LOINC#59284-0 "Patient Consent" * patient = Reference(PilgrimExample) * dateTime = "2025-04-01T09:00:00+08:00" * performer = Reference(PilgrimExample) * organization = Reference(OriginHIEExample) * sourceAttachment.contentType = #text/plain * sourceAttachment.url = "https://hie.mys.example.org/consents/hajj-1446/consent-mys.txt" * sourceAttachment.title = "Consent text shown to the pilgrim: CONSENT-MYS (example)" * policyRule = $IPSHajjConsent|2.1.0#CONSENT-MYS "Consent for Malaysia" * provision.type = #permit * provision.period.start = "2025-05-01" * provision.period.end = "2025-08-31" * provision.actor.role = $v3-ParticipationType#IRCP "information recipient" * provision.actor.reference.identifier.system = "urn:ietf:rfc:3986" * provision.actor.reference.identifier.value = "https://moh.ksa.example.org/" * provision.actor.reference.display = "Ministry of Health Saudi Arabia (example)" * provision.purpose = $v3-ActReason#TREAT "treatment" Instance: PilgrimConsentHostUse InstanceOf: $PCFIntermediate Title: "Pilgrim consent: the host Ministry of Health may use the IPS for care during Hajj" Description: "The second of the pilgrim's two Hajj consents (CONSENT-KSA, host use). Permit, to the host Ministry of Health as information recipient, for treatment, during the example Hajj period and its follow-up. It binds the host Ministry of Health after receipt." Usage: #example * status = #active * scope = $consentscope#patient-privacy * category[0] = $LOINC#59284-0 "Patient Consent" * patient = Reference(PilgrimExample) * dateTime = "2025-04-01T09:05:00+08:00" * performer = Reference(PilgrimExample) * organization = Reference(OriginHIEExample) * sourceAttachment.contentType = #text/plain * sourceAttachment.url = "https://hie.mys.example.org/consents/hajj-1446/consent-ksa.txt" * sourceAttachment.title = "Consent text shown to the pilgrim: CONSENT-KSA (example)" * policyRule = $IPSHajjConsent|2.1.0#CONSENT-KSA "Consent for Kingdom of Saudi Arabia" * provision.type = #permit * provision.period.start = "2025-05-01" * provision.period.end = "2025-08-31" * provision.actor.role = $v3-ParticipationType#IRCP "information recipient" * provision.actor.reference.identifier.system = "urn:ietf:rfc:3986" * provision.actor.reference.identifier.value = "https://moh.ksa.example.org/" * provision.actor.reference.display = "Ministry of Health Saudi Arabia (example)" * provision.purpose = $v3-ActReason#TREAT "treatment" . How step 10 reads them: the origin HIE takes the active Consent whose policyRule is its own release code (CONSENT-MYS) from its registry (PHW.F.8). It matches provision.actor.reference.identifier against the receiver as verified by trust in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain (PHW.I.2), provision.purpose against the purpose (TREAT; see G5), and provision.period against today. That Consent’s decide() result feeds the default DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess (PHW.F.10). PilgrimConsentHostUse (CONSENT-KSA) binds the host Ministry of Health after receipt and is not part of the origin’s decision. The audit event (PHW.I.9) cites each Consent read, by policyRule code and version and by the id and meta.versionId the registry assigned at PHW.A.5. Open questions for the owner . | G6: approve DS4P obligation codes, or keep KSA’s duties in the CONSENT-KSA text only? | G8: is break the glass in scope now? | . e06ec7806fd2.title: index-ig
e06ec7806fd2.content: . This WHO [insert health domain here] Implementation Guide details how to use Health Level 7 (HL7) Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) for consistent digital representation of [insert health domain here] services. This implementation guide and set of artifacts are still undergoing development. Content is for demonstration purposes only. Summary . This implementation guide includes a machine-readable representation of WHO guidelines for [insert health domain here], as documented in the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for [insert health domain here] (link forthcoming) and explicitly encodes computer-interoperable logic, including data models, terminologies, and logic expressions, in a computable language to support implementation of [insert health domain here] use cases by WHO Member States. The guide is part of the WHO SMART Guidelines approach to support countries to integrate WHO global health and data recommendations into digital systems accurately and consistently. It defines a series of FHIR Resources, Profiles, Extensions, and Terminology based on the WHO [insert health domain here] Digital Adaptation Kit (link forthcoming). Supporting guidance, recommendations, resources, and standards are included in the Bibliography and Dependencies. About this implementation guide . This implementation guide is broken into the following levels of knowledge representation: . | Home - contains references to the guidance, guidelines, policies and recommendations underpinning this implementation guide. | Business Requirements - contains the requirements for this implementation guide including the definition of key concepts, use cases, and a data dictionary. | Data Models and Exchange - contains the data models and data exchange protocols with actors and transactions defined. | Deployment Guidance - contains relevant technical specifications and guidance, testing resources, reference implementation materials, and supporting guidance for adaptation to local contexts. | . This guide is prepared to facilitate digital implementation of WHO [insert health domain here] guidelines by providing FHIR-based computable representations of and implementation guidance for using the key components of the WHO [insert health domain here] digital adaptation kit (DAK): . | Health Interventions & Recommendations | Generic Personas | User Scenarios | Business Processes & Workflows | Core Data Elements | Decision Support Logic | Indicators & Monitoring | Functional & Non-functional Requirements | . This guide is a companion to the Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) and should be used side-by-side with it. Implementers are strongly encouraged to make use of the Digital Adaptation Kit. The focus of this guide is on the explanation and use of the computable artifacts. This guide assumes use of the following resources: . | IPS Patient | CPG ActivityDefinitions . | For a complete listing of the artifacts defined in this implementation guide, refer to the Artifact Index. | A complete offline copy of this implementation guide can be found on the Downloads page. | This Implementation Guide makes use of Clinical Quality Language for the decision support artifacts including the PlanDefinitions and Measures. They are used to express how a calculation should occur and can be used with a CQL engine in order to process the decision or indicator directly from the applicable FHIR resources. Links to this specification, the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Speciciation, and other helpful resources can be found in the Support dropdown. | . Disclaimer . Content is for demonstration purposes only. Summary . This implementation guide includes a machine-readable representation of WHO guidelines for [insert health domain here], as documented in the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for [insert health domain here] (link forthcoming) and explicitly encodes computer-interoperable logic, including data models, terminologies, and logic expressions, in a computable language to support implementation of [insert health domain here] use cases by WHO Member States. The guide is part of the WHO SMART Guidelines approach to support countries to integrate WHO global health and data recommendations into digital systems accurately and consistently. It defines a series of FHIR Resources, Profiles, Extensions, and Terminology based on the WHO [insert health domain here] Digital Adaptation Kit (link forthcoming). Supporting guidance, recommendations, resources, and standards are included in the Bibliography and Dependencies. About this implementation guide . This implementation guide is broken into the following levels of knowledge representation: . | Home - contains references to the guidance, guidelines, policies and recommendations underpinning this implementation guide. | Business Requirements - contains the requirements for this implementation guide including the definition of key concepts, use cases, and a data dictionary. | Data Models and Exchange - contains the data models and data exchange protocols with actors and transactions defined. | Deployment Guidance - contains relevant technical specifications and guidance, testing resources, reference implementation materials, and supporting guidance for adaptation to local contexts. | . This guide is prepared to facilitate digital implementation of WHO [insert health domain here] guidelines by providing FHIR-based computable representations of and implementation guidance for using the key components of the WHO [insert health domain here] digital adaptation kit (DAK): . | Health Interventions & Recommendations | Generic Personas | User Scenarios | Business Processes & Workflows | Core Data Elements | Decision Support Logic | Indicators & Monitoring | Functional & Non-functional Requirements | . This guide is a companion to the Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) and should be used side-by-side with it. Implementers are strongly encouraged to make use of the Digital Adaptation Kit. The focus of this guide is on the explanation and use of the computable artifacts. This guide assumes use of the following resources: . | IPS Patient | CPG ActivityDefinitions . | For a complete listing of the artifacts defined in this implementation guide, refer to the Artifact Index. | A complete offline copy of this implementation guide can be found on the Downloads page. | This Implementation Guide makes use of Clinical Quality Language for the decision support artifacts including the PlanDefinitions and Measures. They are used to express how a calculation should occur and can be used with a CQL engine in order to process the decision or indicator directly from the applicable FHIR resources. Links to this specification, the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Speciciation, and other helpful resources can be found in the Support dropdown. | . Disclaimer . 241499fb4aed.title: User Scenarios
241499fb4aed.content: . Component 3 in the Digital Adaptation Kit (link forthcoming) includes user scenarios, which are narratives that describe how the different personas may interact with each other. The user scenarios are only illustrative and are intended to give an idea of a typical workflow. How to interpret user scenarios . User scenarios can be helpful tools not only to better understand the context in which a digital tool would operate, but also for some insights into what key data elements would need to be recorded and accounted for in the database. Additionally, the context in which the tool would operate, illuminated by the user scenarios, provides insight into some functional and non-functional requirements that the system would also need. As examples, the scenarios identify: key data elements that need to be recorded and/or calculated; decision-support logic that can be automated in the system; key functional and non-functional requirements that should be included in the system, and adolescent-specific considerations that should be accounted for. 9d17c5846c2c.title: system-requirements
9d17c5846c2c.content: . Functional Requirements . Functional requirements describe the capabilities the system must have in order to meet the end-users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process. These requirements are taken from Component 8 and Web Annex D of the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for [insert health domain here] (link forthcoming). Please note that these are not exhaustive lists and should be modified according to context and user persona needs . Non-functional Requirements . Non-functional requirements provide the general attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. Examples of non-functional requirements include ability to work offline, multiple language settings and password protection. Table 17 in the DAK provides non-functional requirements as general characteristics of the overall system. Edit this page on GitHub . | top . IG © 2023+ WHO. Issuer has performed any necceasry document generation, digital signatures and has generated a VHL according to a content profile .
